translationRepairs: Su Chuo had been in office for more than a year before Grand Progenitor Yuwen Tai truly knew his worth.
Su Chuo had been in office for more than a year, and Grand Progenitor Yuwen Tai did not yet know him deeply.
s0009 太祖未深知之 states that after more than a year Tai still did not know Su Chuo deeply; “before … truly knew his worth” turns the negation into eventual recognition of worth and misstates 未深知.
s0236 contains only the fragment （五）; “[Since the Three Five]” invents a full temporal clause not present in this unit, while “Five” matches the supplied Chinese.
since then, every age has had systems of taxation.
Since the Three, every age has had systems of taxation.

s0237 has 三以來, so “since then” wrongly drops 三; Wikisource restores classical 三五以來 across the split with s0236’s （五）, but this unit’s Chinese alone supports “Since the Three,” not inventing “and Five” again here.
The Pillar of State and all the grandees and ranking generals came to court without exception.
Pillar-of-State Yuwen Tai and all the grandees and ranking generals came to court without exception.
s0263 柱國泰 explicitly names Tai after the title 柱國; omitting that personal name is an error, and “Pillar-of-State Yuwen Tai” accurately identifies him in idiomatic English.
The Pillar of State and all the grandees and ranking generals, none failed to come to court.
Pillar-of-State Tai and all the grandees and ranking generals, none failed to come to court.
The same 柱國泰 requires the name in the literal field; “Pillar-of-State Tai” restores 泰 without adding matter absent from the Chinese.

At the start of Sui's Kaihuang era, because Su Chuo had been famous in the former age, an edict was issued: "In olden days Emperor Gao of Han admired the righteousness of Wang Ling; Emperor Wu of Wei drew upon the spirit of Cao Zigan—former ages' eminent worthies were honored by later kings.

At the start of Sui's Kaihuang era, because Su Chuo had been famous in the former age, an edict was issued: "In olden days Emperor Gao of Han admired the righteousness of Wuji; Emperor Wu of Wei drew upon the spirit of Zigan—former ages' eminent worthies were honored by later kings.
s0379 has 漢高欽無忌之義，魏武挹子幹之風; Wang Ling and the surname Cao are not in the Chinese, and Wuji / Zigan correctly follow 無忌 and 子幹.
On the fourth day of the sixth month the Emperor offered morning rites at the Grand Temple; every officer was in his place.
On day dingsi of the sixth month the Emperor offered morning rites at the Grand Temple; every officer was in his place.
s0270 dates the rites to 六月丁巳, a sexagenary day-name; rendering it as “the fourth day” invents an ordinal month-day the Chinese does not state.
Men like Yiyin the cook, Fuyue the prisoner, Gao Yao who "advanced in planting virtue," and Guan Zhong in humble obscurity are rarely celebrated in their own time;
Men like the cook, the convict laborer, the planter of virtue, and Guan Zhong in humble obscurity are rarely celebrated in their own time;
s0406 lists 庖廚、胥靡、種德、微管 as allusive categories; naming Yiyin, Fuyue, and Gao Yao invents proper names not written in the unit, while keeping Guan Zhong for 微管 matches the clearest abbreviation.
